full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the judgment and order dated 10-11-1997 passed by the Additional District Judge. First Court, Kushtia in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 18 of 1996 allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and order dated 30-5-96 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Khoksha in Miscellaneous Case No. 22 of 1994 under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act dismissing the Miscellaneous Case. 

 2. Facts, in short, are that the present opposite Party No. 1 as petitioner filed Miscellaneous Case No. 22 of 1994 for preemption of the case land under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act against the opposite parties on the assertions that the petitioner of the aforesaid miscellaneous case is the co-sharer of the disputed holding recorded in SA Khatian No. 236 by way of inheritance. The petitioner's co-sharer Dr Aftab Uddin transferred the case land to the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 on the basis of a heba-bil-ewaz deed dated 29-7-93 without any notice to the petitioner. Hence the case upon deposit of an amount of Taka 5,000 together with the statutory compensation. 

 7. There is no dispute that opposite party No. 2 is a co-sharer of opposite No.1 in the disputed holding. It is the definite case of the opposite party No.1 that the petitioners are strangers and that opposite party No. 2 without notice of the transfer in question to the opposite party No.1 made the transaction and that he came to know of the transfer effected by the heba-bil-ewaz only on 11-7-1994. The petitioners, on the other hand, have stated that they are 'mamato' brothers of the transferor opposite party No. 2. It appears from the judgment of the trial Court that he on reference to the oral evidence of the witnesses held that the petitioners are the 'Mamato' brothers of opposite party Nos. 1 and 2. Here the question of relationship by consanguinity comes in for consideration in view of clause (c) of sub-section 10 of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Clause (c) has excepted certain categories of persons who claim interest in a given land by way of heba-bil-ewaz. Clause (c) of section 96 (10) is as under: 

 Mr Nurul Amin, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that in the instant case the heba-bil-ewaz was made by opposite party No. 2 in favour of the petitioner upon receipt of one copy of the Holy Quran, one cap and a Jainamaj (prayer mat). It is contended by him that a copy of the Holy Quran, cap and a jainamaj (prayer mat) do not fall within the purview of pecuniary consideration as indicated in clause (c). They are all on pecuniary consideration and if a transfer is effected by a heba-bil-ewaz in exchange of the above 3 items in favour of a person who happens to be a close relation of the donor within three degrees of consanguinity then the transfer so made will not be liable for preemption. That heba-bil-ewaz effected in exchange of prayer-mat, cap and copy of the Holy Quran is not to be construed as having been made for pecuniary consideration and this has been decided in number of cases and in this connection the learned Advocate of the petitioners refers to the citations reported in 11 DLR 353 in the case of Shafique Mia and others vs Hafizuddin and others, 20 DLR 433 in the case of Syed Ali Gazi and others vs Akhaj Sardar and others, and 44 DLR 228 in the case of Mir Amanullah vs Mohammad Sharif and others. It is further argued by the learned Advocate of the petitioners that non-pecuniary consideration for making a transfer on the basis of a Heba-bil-ewaz will not be enough and the right of preemption of the preemptor cannot be resisted unless the donor and the donee stand in relationship with each other within 3 degrees of consanguinity. It is submitted by him that the petitioners are, as established by evidence on record, 'mamato' brothers Of the donor. Being the 'mamato' brother of the donor, the opposite party No.1 cannot preempt the land demised by the heba-bil-ewaz. To show that the petitioners are within 3 degrees of consanguinity, the learned Advocate of the petitioners refers to a decision reported in 48 DLR (AD) 88 in the case of Shamsu I Islam and others vs Badiuz Zaman@ Bablu and another. It is submitted by him that in the above case it was found by the Appellate Division while interpreting section 96(10)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act that a cousin sister's son is within 3 degree of consanguinity with the donor. It is contended by the learned Counsel for the petitioners that in the instant case the transferees are the maternal uncle's son of the donor which relationship is more nearer in degree to the donor compared to the cousin sister's son as indicated in the aforesaid decision. This being the position the interest of the petitioners acquired by the heba-bil-ewaz in question cannot be preempted. 

 8. Next submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners is on the point of limitation which, as submitted by him, is dependent upon facts. It is submitted by him that the trial Court upon consideration of the evidence held that opposite party No.1 was very much aware of the transfer as well as the possession in the case land. Opposite Party Nos. 1 and 2 both are the residents of Kushtia town. It is contended by the learned Advocate of the petitioners that opposite party No.1 being a resident of Kushtia town like opposite pray No. 2 is stated to have learnt about the transfer from his son PW 1 on 1-7-1994. This fact of knowledge of the transfer has been discussed at length in the judgment of the trial Court after sifting the evidence of the witnesses. It is further argued by the learned Advocate of the petitioners that the lower appellate Court as the final court of facts did not discuss at all the evidence of the witnesses nor did the lower appellate Court dwell upon the evidence of the witnesses adduced on behalf of both the parties. He did not controvert the finding of the trial Court with convincing reasons and the heba-bil-ewaz documents alleged to have been executed by opposite party No. 2 in favour of several persons weighed heavily upon the mind of the lower appellate Court to allow the preemption case of opposite party No. 1. It is submitted by the learned Counsel of the petitioners that these documents have not been used in evidence by any party before the trial Court as well as before the lower appellate Court and there is no knowing as to on what basis the lower appellate Court made mention of these 13 Heba-bil-ewaz documents. It is further contended by the learned Counsel of the petitioners that the lower appellate Court had handed down a judgment which is not a judgment of reversal in the true legal sense of the term and such judgment is not in consonance with the requirements of law as laid down in Order LXI rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure and that, as such, the impugned judgment and order cannot be sustained in law. 

 11. The question now remains to be addressed is whether the petitioners being the done of the heba-bil-ewaz in question are within 3 degrees of consanguinity with the donor ie the opposite party No. 2. This question appears to have been adequately addressed in the decision reported in 48 DLR (AD) 88 wherein their Lordships of the Appellate Division were pleased to hold that cousin sister's son is within three degrees of consanguinity from the donor. In the instant case, the petitioners being the 'Mamato' brothers of opposite party No. 2 who is the donor, they are more nearer in degree with the donor than the cousin sister's son, So, the petitioners in the light of the Appellate Division Judgment are well within 3 degrees of consanguinity from the donor. The petitioners therefore, satisfied all the requirements of law as laid down in section 96(10)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and, as such, the transfer made to them on the basis of the Heba-bil-ewaz in question cannot be preempted. Regarding the question of the case being barred by limitation it is my considered opinion that the trial Court on proper appreciation of the evidence on record rightly held that the case as filed by the opposite party No.1 is barred by limitation. The lower appellate Court has not set aside this finding of the trial Court with sufficient and cogent reason. On perusal of the judgment of the lower appellate Court, I hold the view that the impugned judgment and order is not a proper judgment of reversal as per provisions of law as laid down in Order XLI rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure. To hand down a judgment of reversal, the lower appellate Court is required to consider the judgment and order of the trial Court and then reverse the finding of the trial Court with sufficient and cogent reasons. In my opinion, the judgment and order of the lower appellate Court has been passed in a perfunctory and slipshod manner.
